# Job Chapter 42 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 432r

---

**1** Then Job replied to the LORD: **2** "I know that you can do anything and that no plan of yours can be stopped.

**3** You asked, 'Who is this that obscures my counsel without knowledge?' I was the one. I spoke of things I did not understand — things too wonderful for me to know.

**4** You said, 'Listen, and I will speak. I will question you, and you will answer me.'

**5** I had only heard about you before, but now I have seen you with my own eyes. **6** Therefore I take back everything I said, and I sit in dust and ashes, humbled."

**7** After the LORD had finished speaking to Job, he said to Eliphaz the Temanite: "I am angry with you and your two friends, because you did not speak the truth about me, as my servant Job did.

**8** So now, take seven bulls and seven rams, go to my servant Job, and sacrifice a burnt offering for yourselves. My servant Job will pray for you, and I will accept his prayer and not punish you as your foolishness deserves. For you did not speak the truth about me, as my servant Job did."

**9** So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went and did what the LORD commanded, and the LORD accepted Job's prayer on their behalf.

**10** After Job had prayed for his friends, the LORD restored his fortunes — and gave him twice as much as he had before!

**11** All his brothers and sisters and everyone who had known him before came and ate with him in his house. They expressed their sympathy and comforted him for all the suffering the LORD had allowed. Each one gave him a piece of silver and a gold ring.

**12** The LORD blessed the second half of Job's life even more than the first. He now owned fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand female donkeys.

**13** He also had seven sons and three daughters. **14** He named the first daughter Jemimah, the second Keziah, and the third Keren-Happuch.

**15** Nowhere in the entire land were there women as beautiful as Job's daughters. And their father gave them an inheritance alongside their brothers.

**16** After this, Job lived another hundred and forty years and saw his children and their children to the fourth generation. **17** Then Job died — an old man who had lived a long and full life.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**"Now my eye sees you" (v.5):** This is the answer to the entire book. Not an argument. Not an explanation. An encounter. Job's faith was built on what he had been told about God — tradition, theology, received wisdom. Now, having met God face to face in the whirlwind, everything has changed. The suffering is not explained. The theology is not corrected. But Job is transformed because he has experienced God directly. The book's answer to "Why do the innocent suffer?" is, ultimately, "Come and see."

**The friends rebuked, Job vindicated (v.7):** This is the most shocking verse in the epilogue. The friends spent 29 chapters defending God — and God says they got it wrong. Job spent those same chapters accusing God — and God says he got it right. The word translated "right" (*nekhonah*) means "established, reliable, true." Honest wrestling with God is more faithful than dishonest defense of God. This single verse demolishes every theology that silences doubt in the name of piety.

**Restoration and its limits (vv.10-17):** The epilogue gives Job back double everything — except his children. He receives seven new sons and three new daughters, not fourteen sons and six daughters. The original children cannot be replaced. Some see this as the narrator's refusal to sentimentalize: restoration is real but not complete. The daughters being named (while the sons are not) and receiving inheritance is a remarkable detail — in the ancient world, this signals exceptional honor. The book ends with the simplest possible sentence: "Job died, old and full of days." After 42 chapters of agony and theology, the ending is quiet. That quietness is its own kind of peace.

*— PNEUMA*
